post.title: leguard: Turning Agent Guardrails from Prompt Suggestions into Exit Codes
post.description: How I built leguard, a zero-dependency Bun hook layer enforcing read-before-edit, lint gates, protected paths, and shell policy across nine agent harnesses.
post.excerpt: AI coding agents edit files they never read, leave lint errors behind, and say "done" while the quality gate is red. Prompt rules are probabilistic; hooks run every time. leguard is a zero-dependency Bun/TypeScript hook layer that enforces read-before-edit, post-edit lint, protected paths, and shell-command policy across nine agent harnesses with one contract: exit 2 plus stderr means blocked.
post.content:
Every AI coding agent I run drifts in the same predictable ways. It edits a file it never read. It leaves lint and type errors behind. It declares "done" while the quality gate is red. It wanders into `.env` files and `.git/`. And once in a while it emits a shell command that would ruin my week.

The standard fix is more rules in the system prompt. I kept doing that, and they kept drifting, because prompt instructions are probabilistic. Models forget rules under context pressure, and small local models forget fastest. The thesis in leguard's PLAN.md is the whole project in one line: use prompts for guidance, hooks for behavior that must run every time. Don't make agents remember rules. Make the rules unmissable via lifecycle hooks.

So I built **leguard** (`@lesearch/leguard`, v0.4.0): a zero-dependency Bun and TypeScript hook layer that turns guardrails from suggestions into deterministic machinery. Read-before-edit. Post-edit lint gates. Protected paths. Shell-command policy. The whole thing is roughly 2,264 lines of TypeScript that Bun executes raw: no build step, `node:` builtins only, an empty `devDependencies`.

## Two problems, one layer

Drift is only half of it. The other half is fragmentation. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode each speak a different hook-payload dialect: `tool_name` vs `toolName` vs plain `tool`, `file_path` vs `filePath` vs `target`. Guardrails normally get rewritten per harness.

leguard solves both at once: one enforcement layer, one normalized event shape, any harness.

## The contract: exit 2 plus stderr

Every hook is a standalone Bun script that reads a JSON payload from stdin. Enforcement is pure exit codes. Exit 2 plus a stderr message blocks the tool call, and the agent reads that stderr as ground truth to self-correct against. Exit 0 allows. There is deliberately no warn mode: a warning is just a prompt suggestion wearing a different hat.

## How it works

1. **Harness detection.** `loadEvent()` in `hooks/common.ts` dispatches to nine adapters in `hooks/harnesses/`: claude, codex, cursor, opencode, antigravity, vibe, hermes, ollama, and a catch-all `unknown` that always runs last. Each adapter fingerprints the payload shape. Claude Code announces itself via `hook_event_name` and `transcript_path`, Codex via its lifecycle type strings or the `apply_patch` tool, Hermes via JSON-RPC methods starting with `hooks/`, Ollama via a model-name regex like `/^(qwen|llama|mistral|...)/`. Writing these detectors felt like protocol archaeology.

2. **Normalization.** Every adapter emits the same `HookEvent`: `{harness, lifecycle, sessionId, cwd, tool: {name, input, paths, bashCommand}}`. Field extraction tolerates every spelling (`tool_input`, `toolInput`, `input`, `params`, `arguments`; `file_path`, `filePath`, `path`, `target`, `files[]`). Hook logic never touches raw harness fields.

3. **Read tracking and read-before-edit.** A PostToolUse hook on Read records paths per session in `${TMPDIR}/leguard/reads/<sessionId>.json`. A PreToolUse hook on Edit, Write, and MultiEdit then blocks any edit to an existing file the agent has not read this session. New files pass. This kills the blind-edit failure mode outright.

4. **Protected paths and command policy.** protect-paths regex-denies `.git/`, `.env*`, private keys (`id_rsa`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`), and generated directories like `node_modules`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `.next`, and `.cache`, extensible via `LEGUARD_PROTECTED_GLOBS`. command-policy denies dangerous shell: `rm -rf` on `/` or `~`, `curl | sh`, `cat .env`, `DROP TABLE`, `chmod 777`, force-push to main or master, fork bombs, `mkfs`, and raw `dd` to disk devices, extensible via `LEGUARD_COMMAND_DENY`.

5. **The quality loop.** post-edit-lint runs `biome check --write` on TS, JS, and JSON after every edit (plus `tsgo --noEmit` when `LEGUARD_TYPECHECK=1`). For Rust it computes Cargo package roots upward from the touched files, then runs `cargo fmt` and package-scoped `cargo clippy --no-deps`. Results land in `.hook-state/last-quality-gate.json`. Missing tools skip politely unless `LEGUARD_STRICT_TOOLS=1`.

6. **Stop-if-red.** The Stop hook reads that state file and blocks turn completion while it is red, replaying the failing command output back to the agent. The agent cannot say "done" past a red gate. The loop becomes: agent edits, clippy fails, stderr feeds back, agent fixes, gate goes green.

## Try it

The test suite runs harness detection and normalization against real payload fixtures from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and Hermes, plus hook smoke tests:

```bash
bun test
```

In my clone: 17 pass, 0 fail, 45 assertions, about 258ms on Bun 1.3.14.

```bash
bun run smoke
```

This spawns each hook as a real subprocess with synthetic stdin payloads in a temp dir: it asserts that edit-before-read exits 2, read-then-edit exits 0, and the quality-gate state file gets written. It ends with "leguard smoke test passed".

Wiring it into one test project is a config drop (paths assume the clone lives at `~/Projects/leguard`, adjust to yours):

```bash
mkdir -p .claude .hook-state
cp ~/Projects/leguard/configs/settings.local.claude.json .claude/settings.json
cp ~/Projects/leguard/configs/biome.json ./biome.json
bun add -d -E @biomejs/biome
```

A matching Codex fragment (`configs/hooks.codex.fragment.json`) shares the same shape. Then watch decisions stream:

```bash
tail -f /tmp/leguard/audit.jsonl
```

Every hook invocation appends one JSONL row: hook name, exit code, block/allow/error outcome, duration in milliseconds.

## Design choices you only make at 2am

**Fail-soft, not fail-closed.** Most guard systems fail closed. leguard's `runHook()` wrapper fails open on its own bugs: an uncaught exception logs one line and exits 0. The comment in common.ts says why: "a thrown exception in the hook layer must NEVER deadlock the agent loop." You only make that choice when a hook bug at 3am must not freeze an unattended run.

**The literal `/tmp`.** The audit log is hardcoded to `/tmp/leguard/audit.jsonl` (override: `LEGUARD_AUDIT_PATH`) because on macOS `os.tmpdir()` resolves to `/var/folders/.../T`, so the documented tail path sat silently empty and confused my stress-test verifier. That debugging story is fossilized in a comment.

**Clippy from the file, not the cwd.** post-edit-lint documents its own bug fix: package roots are computed upward from the touched files, because the old cwd-based findUp silently skipped clippy whenever the agent's cwd was not inside the cargo project.

One more hook: on SessionEnd, learning-capture appends transcript tails to `~/.claude/PAI/MEMORY/LEARNING/leguard.jsonl` when trigger phrases like "lesson:" appear. Together with the audit log it is dual-purpose: operational telemetry today, an SFT training-signal stream for small local models tomorrow.

## The agent bus

v0.4.0 also shipped a separate agent bus (`bus/`): serverless Mac-to-VM multi-agent coordination over append-only JSONL plus O_EXCL lock files on a shared filesystem. No daemon, just seven small CLIs (`lg-task-new`, `lg-claim`, `lg-complete`, `lg-msg`, `lg-poll`, `lg-search`, `lg-bg`). Agents claim tasks by winning an exclusive file create.

## Honest limitations

- This is a one-day build: a single commit, created and last pushed on May 21, 2026. The repo is currently private with no LICENSE, which is why there is no GitHub link in this post yet. The v0.4.0 label reflects internal iteration squashed into one commit, not a release history.
- Validation is simulated payloads plus smoke tests. It is not yet wired into my global Claude or Codex config: no extended real-world mileage yet.
- Only 5 of the 9 adapters have real payload fixtures. The Antigravity, Vibe, and Ollama adapters are shape guesses, and the code's own comments say so. The Codex fragment exists but has not been run against a real Codex install.
- command-policy and protect-paths are regex deny-lists over a normalized string. They are guardrails against accidents, not a sandbox. A motivated agent can route around them with encodings, variables, or unlisted spellings.
- The README is stale: still titled "Agent Loop Hooks", and it references old `AGENT_LOOP_*` env names while the code reads `LEGUARD_*`. The smoke script still sets an old `AGENT_LOOP_*` var the code ignores; it passes only because non-strict is the default.
- The lint gate only covers `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.json`, and `.rs`. Learning capture stores the last 120 transcript lines with a hardcoded task label, not structured lesson rows. The root Cargo.toml references a workspace member that is not in the repo. And the session-id fallback to `$USER` could mix read state across concurrent sessions.

## What's next

Flip the repo public with a license so this post can actually link it. Wire leguard into my daily global config, earn real mileage, and capture real payload fixtures for the three speculative adapters. Evolve learning capture into structured `{task, attempt, outcome, lesson}` rows; PLAN.md defers any fine-tuning until 200+ rows exist, and no model has been trained yet.

The endgame is the bet stated in PLAN.md: hooks make multi-agent, Ralph-style loops self-correcting, because each agent sees the deterministic error stream as ground truth. Determinism, not bigger models, is what lets small local models do real coding work. As an Agentic Engineer running loops nobody is watching, I would rather have exit codes than promises.

Your AI coding agent will forget the rules in your prompt. Not maybe: predictably, under context pressure, and small local models forget fastest.

I built leguard, a zero-dependency Bun/TypeScript hook layer that makes the rules unmissable instead of memorable.

Three takeaways from building it:

1. The entire enforcement API is two exit codes. Exit 2 plus stderr means blocked, and the agent treats that message as ground truth and self-corrects. No warn mode, because a warning is just more prompt to ignore.

2. Normalize the harness chaos once. Nine adapters fingerprint payloads from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and others into one HookEvent shape, so every gate (read-before-edit, post-edit lint, protected paths, command policy) is written exactly once.

3. Fail open on your own bugs. A crashed hook logs one line and exits 0, because a hook bug should never deadlock an unattended overnight loop.

It is a one-day build with a single commit, validated by tests and smoke runs, not by production mileage, and the post is honest about that.

What is the one rule you wish your agent could never break?
